source.title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
source.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022)

confidence_rationale: Two-sided by construction, which is why the direction is mixed rather than supports. It is the strongest available methodological warrant for Q-093's insistence on MATCHED-budget comparison -- Chinchilla's whole result exists only because Gopher, GPT-3 and Megatron-Turing NLG were re-compared at equal compute rather than at equal parameter count, and the ranking inverted. But its central empirical finding cuts the other way for the baseline class: for monolithic transformers, capacity and experience must scale EQUALLY, so the comparison class Q-093 must beat is strictly proportional, with no sublinear dividend of its own. Confidence reflects an exceptionally solid result (400+ trained models) applied to a question it was not designed to answer.
failure_signatures: For monolithic transformers the compute-optimal frontier requires model size and training tokens to scale 1:1, so any efficiency dividend REE claims must come from the architectural seam between control and representation -- it cannot come from sitting on a better-tuned scaling curve, because the baseline class already occupies its own optimum.

Chinchilla's parameter count N is undecomposed: a monolithic transformer has no control-machinery-versus-representational-store seam, so this paper cannot supply a baseline MEASUREMENT of the specific ratio Q-093 asks about, only of total capacity against total experience.

The paper's cost variable is pre-training FLOPs alone. Comparing REE against a Chinchilla-optimal baseline on that variable would silently drop most of Q-093's stated cost terms and could produce a verdict that reverses once inference, memory and adaptation are counted.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Under a fixed training-compute budget, model size and number of training tokens should be scaled equally -- for every doubling of parameters the training tokens should also double -- and current large models are substantially undertrained; a 70B model trained on 4x more data (Chinchilla) uniformly outperforms Gopher (280B), GPT-3 (175B), Jurassic-1 (178B) and Megatron-Turing NLG (530B) at the same compute budget.
mapping.ree_translation: This paper does two distinct jobs for Q-093. Methodologically it is the canonical demonstration that comparisons at unmatched budget are not merely weaker but can be RANK-REVERSING -- the same evidence that grounds Q-093's non-degeneracy precondition, and a warning that a REE-versus-baseline claim asserted at unmatched competence would be worthless rather than provisional. Substantively it characterises the baseline: the dominant comparison class exhibits proportional, not sublinear, scaling of capacity against experience, which fixes the bar REE's control machinery would have to clear.
mapping.mapping_caveat: Chinchilla measures a monolithic system with no seam between organising machinery and representational store, so it cannot be treated as a measurement of Q-093's ratio in the baseline -- only of an aggregate. Its cost axis is pre-training FLOPs, a strict subset of Q-093's lifetime-cost definition, so importing the 1:1 rule as 'the baseline scaling law' in a REE comparison would compare unlike denominators. Note also that this result is about the compute-optimal FRONTIER, not about any particular deployed model; a real baseline system is usually off that frontier, which cuts in REE's favour and must not be quietly exploited.
mapping.source_context: Autoregressive transformer language models, 70M to 16B parameters trained on 5B to 500B tokens (400+ models), plus the 70B Chinchilla model; English text.

confidence_components.notes: Source quality near-maximal: very large controlled sweep, immediately and widely replicated in practice. Mapping fidelity is the limiting term -- the paper answers 'how should total capacity trade against total data' and Q-093 asks 'how does the control fraction of capacity trade against representational richness', which is a decomposition the paper never makes.
